_comment: Videos shown under each chapter. Add an entry, commit, done: no build step. `chapters` takes ch01-style prefixes and a video may list several. A video whose chapter does not exist yet is simply not shown.

videos.title: Cells, Genomes, and the Diversity of Life
Are We All Actually Archaea?
videos.description: Where eukaryotes sit relative to the archaea, including the Asgard group the chapter mentions.

videos.title: The Inner Life of the Cell
videos.description: The animation Harvard commissioned to show a white blood cell's interior at molecular scale. Beautiful, and worth knowing that it compresses timescales enormously and leaves out the crowding and thermal jostling that dominate real cytoplasm.

videos.title: The Origin of Cellular Life on Earth
videos.description: The full Szostak lecture behind the RNA world short, and the direct companion to the Blain and Szostak paper filed under this chapter.

videos.title: The RNA World Hypothesis
videos.description: Jack Szostak, in six minutes, on why RNA is the plausible first replicator.

videos.title: Origin of the eukaryotic cell
videos.description: Nick Lane on where mitochondria came from and why that one event may be the reason complex cells exist at all. He argues a specific and contested position rather than surveying the field, which is what makes it worth the time next to the chapter's short treatment of organelles.

videos.title: HIV Life Cycle
videos.description: A virus running the whole cycle: entry, reverse transcription, integration into the host genome, and assembly of new particles. The chapter treats viruses partly as mobile genetic elements, and this is that idea moving.

videos.title: Model Organisms in Biomedical Research
videos.description: Why a fruit fly or a yeast cell is used to answer questions about humans, and how far the answers carry. The chapter introduces the standard model organisms and the deck leans on them heavily, but the book says little about the reasoning behind the choice.

videos.title: The Genome as the Modern Rosetta Stone
videos.description: Rob Phillips (Caltech) on how much of a sequenced genome we still cannot read: the regulatory DNA between the genes, whose function is largely unknown. A useful corrective to the chapter's account of what having a genome sequence actually buys you.

videos.title: Biochemical Reactions, Enzymes, and ATP
videos.description: MIT 7.01SC, covering free energy, coupled reactions and why ATP hydrolysis drives what it drives.

videos.title: AlphaFold: The Most Useful Thing AI Has Ever Done
videos.description: The deep-learning turn the chapter mentions in a sentence and does not explain.

videos.title: Discovering Kinesin
videos.description: Ron Vale on finding the motor the chapter opens by naming. A good account of what the experiments actually looked like.

videos.title: How Enzymes Work
videos.description: Transition-state stabilisation shown on real structures rather than schematics.

videos.title: Liquid Phase Separation in Living Cells
videos.description: Cliff Brangwynne on biomolecular condensates, which the chapter introduces late and briefly.

videos.title: Molecular Motor Proteins
videos.description: The lecture version: how a shape change plus ATP hydrolysis becomes directed movement.

videos.title: The Protein Folding Revolution
videos.description: Why folding was considered intractable, which is the setup the chapter's last section pays off.

videos.title: What is a Protein?
videos.description: Primary through quaternary structure, built up on actual PDB entries.

videos.title: Reversible Protein Phosphorylation as a Regulatory Mechanism
videos.description: Edmond Fischer on the discovery he shared a Nobel for: that adding and removing a phosphate is how a cell switches a protein on and off. The single most-used idea in the chapter's regulation section, told by one of the people who found it.

videos.title: Prion Disease
videos.description: Susan Lindquist (MIT/HHMI) on a protein whose misfolded form is infectious because it makes other copies misfold the same way. The chapter's amyloid and prion material from a researcher who spent a career on it.

videos.title: Ras oncogene
videos.description: Alfred Wittinghofer (MPI) on Ras as a molecular switch: bound GTP means on, hydrolysis to GDP means off, and a mutation that blocks the hydrolysis leaves it jammed on. Five minutes, and the structural basis for the chapter's GTPase switch.

videos.title: T-State and R-State of Hemoglobin
videos.description: Allostery in the example the chapter builds it on: two conformations, and binding at one site shifting the whole molecule's affinity at the others. Worth watching before the chapter's allosteric enzymes, since hemoglobin is where the idea is easiest to see.

videos.title: Ubiquitination of Proteins
videos.description: How a protein gets tagged for destruction, and why the tag is a chain rather than a single mark. The chapter's control-by-degradation thread, which the deck returns to repeatedly.

videos.title: How Cells Read the Genome: From DNA to Protein
Membrane Transport & Electrical Properties of Membranes
Electron Transport Chain
videos.description: Stage 3 of catabolism, which chapter 2 names and chapter 14 explains.

videos.title: Synthesis of ATP
videos.description: Drew Berry's animation of ATP synthase turning. The rotary mechanism is far easier to believe once you have watched it.

videos.title: Overview of the citric acid cycle
videos.description: Four and a half minutes on the cycle as a whole: what goes in, what comes out, and why the carbons end up as CO2 while the energy leaves on carriers. Start here before the long one below.

videos.title: Metabolism | The Krebs Cycle
videos.description: The whiteboard version, enzyme by enzyme and intermediate by intermediate. Far more detail than the chapter asks for, which is the point when a step stops making sense.

videos.title: Electron carrier molecules
videos.description: NAD+/NADH and FAD/FADH2 as the chapter's activated carriers: what is actually being carried, and why a reduced carrier is a way of holding energy until something needs it.

videos.title: ATP hydrolysis mechanism
videos.description: Why ATP to ADP releases usable energy, at the level of the bond rather than the slogan. The chapter leans on ATP as the cell's currency constantly and explains this once.

videos.title: Muscle metabolism
videos.description: A biochemistry lecturer's account of how muscle actually pays for contraction: which pathway is used over what timescale, and why the fast one runs without oxygen and yields so much less ATP. This is the chapter's aerobic/anaerobic distinction at the level of the pathways rather than the training plan.

videos.title: Overview of Lactate Formation and Recycling
videos.description: Where pyruvate goes when it cannot be oxidised fast enough, why regenerating NAD+ is the actual point of making lactate, and how the liver buys it back through the Cori cycle. The chapter's fermentation section in more detail, and the corrective to the lactic-acid-causes-soreness story.

videos.title: Cell Junctions, Cell Adhesion, & Extracellular Matrix
Cancer
videos.description: The playlist numbers this one Chapter 23; it is chapter 20 in the 7th edition.

videos.title: Pathogens, Infection, and Innate Immunity
videos.description: The playlist numbers this one Chapter 24; it spans chapter 23 and the innate half of chapter 24 in the 7th edition.

videos.title: The Adaptive Immune System
videos.description: The playlist numbers this one Chapter 20; it covers the adaptive half of chapter 24 in the 7th edition.

videos.title: Matthew Meselson: The Semi-Conservative Replication of DNA
videos.description: Meselson telling his own experiment, which is the evidence for the semiconservative replication the chapter asserts in a sentence. Direct companion to the Meselson and Stahl paper filed under this chapter.

videos.title: Chromosomal DNA Replication: Initiation of DNA Replication
videos.description: Stephen Bell on ORC, helicase loading and licensing. The chapter compresses the once-and-only-once problem into two paragraphs; this is the version with the experiments in it.

videos.title: Investigating How DNA Replication Initiates in Eukaryotes
videos.source: Int'l Centre for Genetic Eng. and Biotechnology
videos.description: John Diffley on rebuilding eukaryotic origin firing from purified proteins. Watch after the Bell talk: this is what it took to prove the licensing model rather than infer it.

videos.title: DNA Topology and the Mechanism of Type II DNA Topoisomerases
videos.description: Anthony Maxwell on how a type II enzyme passes one helix through another, and on why trapping it mid-cycle is what makes the fluoroquinolone antibiotics lethal.

videos.title: Paul Modrich: Mechanisms in E. coli and Human Mismatch Repair
videos.description: The 2015 Nobel lecture, and one of the chapter's own references. Modrich on how the strand-discrimination problem was actually solved, first with GATC methylation in bacteria and then without it in humans.

videos.title: Aziz Sancar: Mechanisms of DNA Repair by Photolyase and Excision Nuclease
videos.description: The companion 2015 Nobel lecture, also in the chapter's reference list. Nucleotide excision repair from the person who purified the machinery, including the transcription coupling that Cockayne syndrome breaks.

videos.title: DNA Break Repair by Homologous Recombination
videos.description: Drew Berry's animation of resection, strand invasion and repair synthesis. Worth pairing with Figure 5-47 because the strand dance is much easier to follow moving than drawn.

videos.title: How Do Little Chromosomes Know That They Are Little?
videos.description: Scott Keeney on crossover control, which the chapter calls fascinating and poorly understood before moving on. The guarantee that even the smallest chromosome gets one crossover is the question this whole talk is about.

videos.title: Elizabeth Blackburn: Discovery of Telomeric DNA and Telomerase
videos.description: Blackburn on finding the repeats in Tetrahymena and then the enzyme that makes them, which is the organism and the reaction drawn in Figure 5-34.

videos.title: Virology Lectures 2023 #9: Reverse Transcription and Integration
videos.description: Vincent Racaniello's undergraduate virology course on how a retroviral genome becomes DNA and gets integrated. The chapter gives integrase one sentence; this is the mechanism.

videos.title: TWiV 935: Mobile DNA with Cedric Feschotte
videos.description: A long conversation with a researcher who works on transposable elements and their domestication, covering what half of the human genome is doing and which elements are still moving.

videos.title: Evolution of Replication and Transcription Error Rates Across the Tree of Life
videos.description: Michael Lynch on why mutation rates are the values they are rather than lower. The chapter says a low rate is necessary for life as we know it; this asks what stops selection driving it lower still.
